stem: Describe how the First World War affected Russia before 1917.

points.description: Military defeats (e.g. Tannenberg 1914; losses in 1915) and huge casualties.
Shortages of weapons and supplies for the army.
Food and fuel shortages in the cities; railways overloaded; inflation.
The Tsar took command (1915) and was blamed; Tsarina and Rasputin discredited the government.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The army suffered heavy defeats, such as Tannenberg in 1914 and the losses of 1915, and millions of soldiers were killed, wounded or captured, partly because of shortages of rifles and shells. At home the railways could not carry both troops and food, so the cities ran short of bread and fuel and prices rose much faster than wages. In 1915 the Tsar made himself Commander-in-Chief, so he was blamed for defeats, while the Tsarina and Rasputin discredited the government in Petrograd.

stem: Explain why Lenin's April Theses were important.

points.description: Identifies refusal to support the Provisional Government / 'All power to the Soviets'.
Explains that this made the Bolsheviks the only major party opposing the government, so they gained when it failed.
Identifies the promise of peace and land.
Explains that 'Peace, Land and Bread' matched what soldiers, peasants and workers wanted, winning support.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In the April Theses Lenin told the Bolsheviks to give no support to the Provisional Government and to demand all power to the soviets. This made them the main party opposing the government, so they gained support whenever it failed. He also demanded an end to the war and the transfer of land, summed up as 'Peace, Land and Bread', which matched exactly what soldiers, peasants and workers wanted.

hints: What did Lenin tell his party to do, and what did he promise?

stem: Explain why the Provisional Government failed in 1917.

points.description: Identifies continuing the war.
Explains that the failed summer offensive caused desertion and anger, while the Bolsheviks promised peace.
Identifies delay over land and elections.
Explains that peasants seized land anyway and the government looked weak and unrepresentative.
Identifies dual power / the Kornilov affair.
Explains that Order No. 1 limited its control of the army and Kornilov's failure forced Kerensky to arm the Bolsheviks.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The Provisional Government kept Russia in the war, and when Kerensky's summer offensive failed soldiers deserted and anger grew, while the Bolsheviks promised peace. It postponed land reform and elections to the Constituent Assembly, so peasants seized land anyway and the government, which had never been elected, looked weak. It also never controlled the army fully, because the Soviet's Order No. 1 told soldiers to obey the Soviet first; and in the Kornilov affair Kerensky had to arm the workers, including the Bolshevik Red Guards, who later used those weapons against him.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a letter by a fictional Russian soldier at the front to his family in a village near Tambov, October 1917 (old style) (invented for this question)

> They tell us to hold the line for Russia and the Allies, but we have no boots and the bread is mouldy. In the village, you write, the landlord's fields stand idle and the committee does nothing. The Bolshevik who came to our regiment said: peace now, and the land to those who work it. Half the men listened. I think we will not stay here through the winter.

**Source B** — an editorial in a fictional liberal Petrograd newspaper, the morning after the Winter Palace was captured (invented for this question)

> A handful of armed men, obeying one party, have seized the capital in the name of the soviets while the Congress of Soviets was still meeting. The Constituent Assembly, for which the people have waited since March, has been robbed of its task before it could meet. What was done last night was not the will of Russia but the will of Mr Lenin.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What can you learn from Source A about why the Bolsheviks gained support?

points.description: Soldiers wanted peace; conditions at the front were terrible.
Peasants wanted land; the Bolsheviks promised peace and land while the government delayed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far do Sources A and B give different views of the Bolshevik seizure of power?

points.description: A: suggests real support among soldiers for Bolshevik promises.
B: presents it as a coup by a small armed group of one party.
B: stresses that it pre-empted the Congress and the Constituent Assembly; A says nothing about elections.
Some agreement: both suggest the government's position was weak / it had lost control.

parts.explanation: Differences and any similarity, each supported.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How far do these sources show that the October (November) Revolution was a popular revolution? Use the sources and your own knowledge.

points.description: A: support for Bolshevik slogans among soldiers (own knowledge: majorities in the soviets by September).
A: one soldier's private letter; 'half the men' shows support was not universal.
B: a coup by a small armed force (own knowledge: Military Revolutionary Committee; Red Guards).
B: liberal paper hostile to Bolsheviks; written immediately in anger.
Own knowledge: Bolsheviks won only about a quarter of the Constituent Assembly vote.
Supported judgement.

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source A suggests popular support: a soldier reports that half his regiment listened to a Bolshevik promising peace and land, and my own knowledge shows that by September the Bolsheviks had majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets. But it is one private letter, and 'half the men' shows that support was not universal. Source B presents the seizure as a coup by a small armed force obeying one party, and my own knowledge supports this: the rising was organised by Trotsky's Military Revolutionary Committee before the Congress of Soviets could decide. However, B comes from a liberal paper hostile to the Bolsheviks, written in anger. In the Constituent Assembly elections soon after, the Bolsheviks won only about a quarter of the vote. The sources show that the Bolsheviks had real support for their promises, but that the seizure itself was a coup carried out at a moment when few would defend the government.

parts.explanation: Both sides from the sources, with own knowledge and a judgement.

hints: Consider who wrote each source and what each wanted.

parts.stem: Describe the events of the February (March) Revolution of 1917.

points.description: Women queueing for bread joined striking workers on International Women's Day (8 March / 23 February).
A general strike spread through Petrograd.
Soldiers of the garrison refused to fire and joined the crowds; Petrograd Soviet and Duma committee formed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far was the First World War responsible for the fall of the Tsar in 1917?

points.description: For: military defeats and casualties; the Tsar personally blamed after taking command
For: shortages, inflation and transport breakdown; Tsarina and Rasputin discredited government
Against: long-term weaknesses: autocracy, peasant land hunger, workers' conditions, broken promises of 1905
Against: Nicholas II's own failings; the mutiny of the Petrograd garrison as the decisive event
Supported judgement

Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The war was the main reason the Tsar fell in 1917. Defeats such as Tannenberg and the huge losses of 1915 destroyed confidence in the regime, and after Nicholas took personal command in 1915 he was blamed for every failure. At home, the war overloaded the railways, causing bread and fuel shortages and rapid inflation in the cities, while the Tsarina and Rasputin made the government look incompetent and even disloyal.

However, the war worked on weaknesses that already existed. Russia was an autocracy whose ruler had broken the promises of 1905; peasants still wanted land, workers lived in poor conditions, and strikes were rising before 1914. Nicholas's own stubbornness and poor judgement made things worse, and the decisive moment came when the soldiers of the Petrograd garrison refused to fire on the crowds.

Overall, the war was the most important cause because it turned long-standing discontent into a crisis and turned the army against the Tsar, but it caused his fall only because the regime was already weak.

parts.explanation: Levels: both sides with a supported judgement for the top level.

hints: In (b), compare the war with longer-term weaknesses and the events of early 1917.
